what: Every go test terminal shows a bare `go test` / `go test -v` / `go test ./...`, but the real command pipes the output through a sed that rewrites the package time to …s (and the ./... run also adds -count=1). The rewrite is explained in prose, not in the shown command, which breaks the AUTHORING house rule. Already listed in INTEGRATION_TODO under "From go ch15 (Libraries and Answer Keys)" (HOUSE-RULE CHECK); the evidence below confirms it is still open.
evidence: /home/you/go-ch15/t_first.cmd: shown "go test", real "cd calc && go test | sed -E 's/\t[0-9]+\.[0-9]+s$/\t…s/'; exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}". all_pkgs.cmd: shown "go test ./...", real "cd school && go test -count=1 ./... | sed -E ...". data/go-ch15.json steps[].cmd for t_first.go, mk_*.go, errorf.go, fatal.go, rp_table.go, table_pass.go, example_*.go, vet_fail.go, never_fail.go, boss_spot.go, boss_parsons.go, parsons_aaa.go, fill_*.go and all_pkgs.go all record the bare command. what: Boss 6 asks for the exact wording of the error, but panel 12 and the notebook teach that the same mistake is worded either "undefined: pkg.name" or "name … not exported by package …" depending on whether the compiler inlined a caller. A reader can't tell which from the source, and the predict widget only accepts an exact match.
evidence: ex-b6-m: "answer": "undefined: plants.water", ask "Type the error text that comes after ./main.go:7:9:". P12: "Sometimes the same mistake is worded undefined: shop.bagFee instead … It depends on what Go remembers about the other room". The notebook confirms that inlining decides it (I checked: adding //go:noinline to Total in a scratch copy of market_fee turns the message into "undefined: shop.bagFee"). comic-widgets.js predict: `ok = mine === real`.
fix: Ask for something the reader can work out, e.g. "Type the name Go refuses, as it appears after the colon" with answer "plants.water" (it appears in stderr), or turn it into a choice: "Does the build succeed? Which line does Go refuse, and why?"

panel: notebook, Under the hood (What an open file is)
what: Says each program gets often 1024 open files on Linux. Since Go 1.19, Go programs on Unix raise their soft open-file limit to the hard limit at startup, so 1024 is misleading for Go.
evidence: Notebook: "Each program gets a limited number of them (often 1024 by default on Linux)". In a scratch test with `ulimit -Sn 1024` in the shell, a Go 1.27.3 program reading syscall.Getrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE) printed "19999 20000" (soft raised to near the hard limit). The Go 1.19 release notes describe this automatic raise (cited from memory, not fetched).
fix: "Each program gets a limited number of them (the operating system sets the limit; Go raises it as far as it may at startup)".

what: The explanation of `main.arrow(0x56c278?)` doesn't say why the argument isn't 7, or what the `?` means. A beginner who just called arrow(7) will be confused.
evidence: Capture impossible.go: "main.arrow(0x56c278?)" for the call arrow(7). P42: "The 0x56c278? next to arrow is a peek at its argument as raw memory; it differs from run to run of different builds. Ignore it."
fix: "…is Go's best guess at the argument. The ? means it may be stale: here the 7 had already been overwritten, so the number is meaningless. Ignore it."

what: The Lab says Go 1.26 or later is all you need for new(42). But Go 1.26's go mod init writes `go 1.25.0` into go.mod, so a reader on Go 1.26.x following the Lab hits panel 23's error.
evidence: Lab: "For new(42) you need Go 1.26 or later; everything else here works on older versions too." Go 1.26 release notes (go.dev/doc/go1.26): "Go 1.26 and its minor releases will create go.mod files with go 1.25.0." (This book's Go 1.27.3 writes go 1.27.3, so the captures are unaffected.)
fix: "For new(42) you need Go 1.26 or later, and a go.mod whose go line says 1.26 or later (if go mod init wrote an older one, run go mod edit -go=1.26)."
